about.pronunciation:
Ecclesiastical (Italianate) pronunciation, the pronunciation used at Mass. There is no audio here.

  • c before e, i, ae, oe, y is “ch” as in church (caelum, peccāta). Otherwise c is “k” (confiteor).
  • g before e or i is “j” as in gem (genitum). Otherwise g is hard (glōria).
  • ae and oe are pronounced “e” (caelum like “che-lum,” saecula like “se-cu-la”).
  • ti before a vowel is “tsi,” unless it follows s, t, or x (grātia “gra-tsia”; iūstus keeps “ti”).
  • gn is “ny” (magnam “ma-nyam,” Agnus “a-nyus”).
  • sc before e or i is “sh” (dēscendit “de-shen-dit”).
  • h is silent (hōsanna, homō). ph is “f” (prophēta). th is “t.”
  • The stressed syllable is the same one as in classical Latin. Macrons in this app mark long vowels; a printed missal does not print them.
about.sources: Church Latin, tier 1, is the people’s and priest’s fixed parts of the Ordinary of the Mass. The Latin is the text of the Missale Romanum before 1931 (the 1920 typical edition and the Ordinary as it stood in that book), which is in the public domain. Biblical sentences follow the Clementine Vulgate. Meanings and usage were checked against H. J. Nunn, An Introduction to Ecclesiastical Latin (1922), C. H. Beeson, A Primer of Medieval Latin (1925), and J. M. Harden, Dictionary of the Vulgate New Testament (1921). The English under each line is a new literal translation made for this app. The Nova Vulgata and the current Missal were not used as sources. Where today’s Ordinary differs, the lesson notes quote only a short phrase.

lines.en: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
The Lord be with you.
And with your spirit.
I confess to almighty God, to blessed Mary ever Virgin, to blessed Michael the Archangel, to blessed John the Baptist, to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to all the saints, and to you, brothers,
that I have sinned exceedingly in thought, word, and deed: through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault.

Therefore I ask blessed Mary ever Virgin, blessed Michael the Archangel, blessed John the Baptist, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the saints, and you, brothers, to pray for me to the Lord our God.
May almighty God have mercy on you, and, with your sins forgiven, lead you to eternal life. Amen.
May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us pardon, absolution, and remission of our sins. Amen.
Lord, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
Glory to God in the highest. And on earth peace to people of good will.
We praise you. We bless you. We worship you. We glorify you.
We give you thanks for your great glory.
Lord God, heavenly King, God the Father almighty.
Lord Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son. Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father.
You who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. You who take away the sins of the world, receive our prayer. You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us.
For you alone are holy. You alone are the Lord. You alone are the Most High, Jesus Christ. With the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen.

texts.title: The Creed: the Father and the Son

lines.en: I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.
And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born of the Father before all ages.
God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father: through whom all things were made.
Who for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven.
And was incarnate by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, and was made man.

texts.title: The Creed: the Passion, the Spirit, and the Church

lines.en: He was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate; he suffered and was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures,
and ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. And he will come again with glory, to judge the living and the dead, whose kingdom will have no end.
And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life: who proceeds from the Father and the Son.
Who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified together: who has spoken through the prophets.
And in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the forgiveness of sins.
And I look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the age to come. Amen.
Pray, brothers, that my sacrifice and yours may become acceptable in the presence of God the Father almighty.
May the Lord receive the sacrifice from your hands, to the praise and glory of his name, and to our benefit too, and that of all his holy Church.
The Lord be with you. And with your spirit.
Up with your hearts. We have them with the Lord.
Let us give thanks to the Lord our God. It is right and just.
Holy, holy, holy Lord God of hosts. Heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest.
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.
Our Father, who art in heaven: hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
Deliver us, we beg, Lord, from all evils, past, present, and to come:
and at the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, with your blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and Andrew, and all the saints,
graciously give peace in our days: so that, helped by the aid of your mercy, we may always be free from sin and safe from every disturbance.
For ever and ever. Amen.
The peace of the Lord be with you always. And with your spirit.
Lamb of God, you who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.
Lamb of God, you who take away the sins of the world, grant us peace.
Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.
Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.
Go, it is the dismissal. Thanks be to God.
May almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

lessons.title: Sign of the Cross and the greeting
lessons.sum: In nōmine Patris, and Dominus vōbīscum.
lessons.notes:
The Sign of the Cross names the Trinity in the genitive: in nōmine “in the name,” then Patris, Fīliī, Spīritūs Sānctī “of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Spirit.” Fīliī is the genitive of fīlius. Spīritus is 4th declension, so its genitive is spīritūs.

Dominus vōbīscum is Dominus plus vōbīs (ablative of vōs) and cum written as one word: “the Lord be with you.” The answer et cum spīritū tuō uses the ablative again: “and with your spirit.”

Ecclesiastical pronunciation, in brief: c before e or i is “ch”; ae and oe are “e”; ti before a vowel is “tsi”; h is silent. The full note is on the About tab.
lessons.diff: The greeting is the same in the current Ordinary. The prayers at the foot of the altar (Introībō ad altāre Deī, Psalm 42) are not. Those belong to the older Missal only and are not in this lesson.

qs: In nōmine Patris, what case is Patris?

lessons.title: The Confiteor
lessons.sum: I confess, and the prayer for pardon.
lessons.notes:
Cōnfiteor takes the dative of the person confessed to: Deō omnipotentī, beātae Māriae, vōbīs. The list of saints is dative too (Mīchaēlī, Iōannī, Apostolīs Petrō et Paulō). Then the construction changes: precor … ōrāre “I ask … to pray,” and those same names become accusative (Māriam, Mīchaēlem, Petrum et Paulum).

Mea culpa is nominative: “my fault,” said three times, the last time maxima “greatest.” Cōgitātiōne, verbō, opere are ablatives of respect: “in thought, in word, in deed.”

Dīmissīs peccātīs vestrīs is an ablative absolute: “your sins having been forgiven.” Misereātur and perdūcat and tribuat are present subjunctives of wishing: “may he have mercy, may he lead, may he grant.”

Vestrī in misereātur vestrī is the objective genitive of vōs (“mercy on you”). This app’s chart shows vestrum first and accepts vestrī. The Missal uses vestrī.
lessons.diff:
The priest’s Confiteor is this same prayer with tibi, pater and te, pater where the server says vōbīs, frātrēs and vōs, frātrēs. Said to one person, the answer is Misereātur tuī … tē.

The current Ordinary uses a shorter Confiteor. It keeps quia peccāvī nimis and mea culpa, adds the short phrase et omissiōne, and says omnēs Angelōs et Sānctōs instead of naming Michael, John, Peter, and Paul.

lessons.title: Kyrie and Gloria
lessons.sum: Lord, have mercy, and Glory to God.
lessons.notes:
Kyrie and eleison are Greek, not Latin, kept as fixed formulas. Chrīste is the vocative of Chrīstus. In the older Mass each of the three invocations is said three times.

The Gloria is a string of short sentences. Glōria and pāx are nominative; Deō and hominibus are dative (“glory to God,” “peace to people”). Bonae voluntātis is genitive: “of good will.”

Laudāmus, benedīcimus, adōrāmus, glōrificāmus are first person plural. Tē is the accusative of tū. Grātiās agimus is the ordinary idiom “we give thanks.” Miserēre is the imperative of misereor. Sōlus agrees with the implied “you”: tū sōlus Sānctus.

The Missal’s ad dexteram is the feminine of dexter “the right hand.” This app shows dextram as the standard form and accepts dexteram.
lessons.diff: The Latin of the Gloria is the same in the current Ordinary. The Kyrie uses the same Greek words; the older book has each invocation three times.

qs: Greek, kept in the Latin Mass

lessons.title: The Creed, part 1
lessons.sum: From Crēdō in ūnum Deum through et homō factus est.
lessons.notes:
Crēdō in plus the accusative is “I believe in.” The objects stay accusative down the list: ūnum Deum, Patrem, factōrem, ūnum Dominum Iēsum Chrīstum.

Genitum, nōn factum “begotten, not made”: genitum is from gignō, factum from faciō. Cōnsubstantiālem Patrī is “of one substance with the Father,” with Patrī in the dative. Per quem omnia facta sunt “through whom all things were made”: facta sunt is the perfect of fīō, used as the passive of faciō.

Et incarnātus est “and he was made flesh,” perfect passive of incarnō. Ex Māriā Virgine is ablative. Homō factus est “he was made man”: homō is nominative, a predicate with factus est.
lessons.diff: The Latin Creed in the current Ordinary is this same Nicene text, still beginning Crēdō, not a plural “we believe.”

qs: Crēdō in ūnum Deum: Deum is
Facta sunt in per quem omnia facta sunt is
Ex Māriā Virgine: the names are

lessons.title: The Creed, part 2
lessons.sum: The Passion, the Spirit, and the Church.
lessons.notes:
Crucifīxus, passus, sepultus are perfect participles with est: “he was crucified, he suffered, he was buried.” Sub Pontiō Pīlātō is ablative, “under Pontius Pilate.” Tertiā diē is ablative of time, “on the third day.” Secundum Scrīptūrās is the preposition secundum with the accusative, “according to the Scriptures.”

Ventūrus est is the future participle of veniō with est: “he is going to come.” Iūdicāre is an infinitive of purpose, “to judge.” Cuius rēgnī nōn erit fīnis “of whose kingdom there will not be an end”: erit is the future of sum.

Fīliōque is Fīliō (ablative of fīlius) plus the enclitic -que “and.” Vīvificantem agrees with Spīritum, “the Spirit who gives life.” The last sentences return to cōnfiteor and exspectō with accusative objects.
lessons.diff: This half of the Creed is the same Latin text in the current Ordinary, including Fīliōque.

qs: he will come / is about to come

lessons.title: Orate fratres and Sursum corda
lessons.sum: The offering, then the preface dialogue.
lessons.notes:
Ōrāte is the plural imperative, addressed to frātrēs in the vocative. Ut … fiat is a purpose clause with the subjunctive of fīō: “that it may become.” Meum ac vestrum “mine and yours”: ac is the short form of atque, and both possessives agree with sacrificium.

The answer Suscipiat is a wish in the subjunctive: “may the Lord receive.” Tōtīusque is the genitive of tōtus (tōtīus, the pronoun-like genitive) plus -que.

Sūrsum corda is “hearts up.” Corda is the neuter plural of cor. Habēmus ad Dominum answers “we have (them) with the Lord.” Agāmus is a hortatory subjunctive, “let us give thanks.” Dignum et iūstum est “it is right and just,” neuter because it describes the action.
lessons.diff: Both the invitation Ōrāte, frātrēs and the Sūrsum corda dialogue have the same Latin wording in the current Ordinary.

lessons.title: Sanctus and Benedictus
lessons.sum: Holy, holy, holy, and Blessed is he who comes.
lessons.notes:
Sānctus is said three times, agreeing with Dominus. Sabaōth is a Hebrew word, “armies, hosts,” left unchanged: Deus Sabaōth “God of hosts.”

Plēnī sunt caelī et terra “heaven and earth are full.” Plēnī is masculine plural with caelī; terra is included in the same predicate. Glōriā tuā is ablative, “with your glory.”

Benedictus quī venit “blessed is he who comes.” Benedictus is the perfect passive participle of benedīcō. In nōmine Dominī is ablative plus a genitive, “in the name of the Lord.” Hōsanna is another Hebrew cry, indeclinable.
lessons.diff: The Sanctus and Benedictus are the same text in the current Ordinary. After the consecration the current Mass adds an acclamation that the older Missal does not have. One of its forms begins Mortem tuam annuntiāmus, Domine.

qs: a Hebrew word meaning hosts or armies

lessons.title: The Lord’s Prayer and the embolism
lessons.notes:
The petitions are subjunctive: sānctificētur “may it be hallowed,” adveniat “may it come,” fiat “may it be done,” nē indūcās “do not lead.” Dā and dīmitte and līberā are imperatives. Dēbita “debts” is the word the Latin Our Father uses, from the Gospel, not a separate word for “trespasses.”

The embolism is the priest’s expansion of the last petition. Quaesumus is the “we” form of defective quaesō “I beg”; those two forms are the ones in ordinary use. Ab omnibus malīs, praeteritīs, praesentibus, et futūrīs is ablative, “from all evils, past, present, and future.”

Intercēdente … Virgine … Genetrice Māriā is another ablative absolute: “with the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, interceding.” Ope misericordiae tuae adiūtī “helped by the aid of your mercy”: ope is the ablative of ops, and adiūtī agrees with “we.”

The people’s answer in this book is Per omnia saecula saeculōrum “through all ages of ages,” then Āmēn.
lessons.diff:
The Our Father itself is the same text. The older embolism names beātā et glōriōsā semper Virgine Deī Genetrice Māriā and Petrō et Paulō, atque Andreā. The current prayer does not.

The older book does not give the people a doxology of their own. The current Ordinary adds one, beginning Quia tuum est rēgnum. What this lesson prints is the 1920 conclusion, Per omnia saecula saeculōrum.

qs: Dēbita nostra in the Our Father means

lessons.title: Peace, communion, and the dismissal
lessons.sum: Pax, Agnus Deī, Ecce Agnus Deī, Īte missa est.
lessons.notes:
Pax Dominī sit semper vōbīscum uses a subjunctive of wishing again: “may the peace of the Lord be with you always.”

The Agnus Dei addresses Agnus Deī in the vocative-like nominative of address, then quī tollis “you who take away,” second person because tollis is second person. The first two end miserēre nōbīs; the third is dā nōbīs pācem “give us peace.” Dā is the imperative of dō, dare. Printed missals show no macron; the long ā is the standard form of that imperative.

Nōn sum dignus ut intrēs “I am not worthy that you should enter,” with ut and the subjunctive. Sub tēctum meum “under my roof,” accusative after sub of motion. Tantum dīc verbō “only say it with a word”: verbō is ablative. Sānābitur is future passive, “will be healed.”

Īte, missa est “go, it is the dismissal.” Missa is a noun from mittō, “a sending away.” Deō grātiās “thanks to God,” dative plus the accusative plural of grātia. The blessing is another wish: Benedīcat vōs “may he bless you.”
lessons.diff:
The older Domine, nōn sum dignus is said three times. The current Ordinary says it once, and the priest adds Beātī quī ad cēnam Agnī vocātī sunt.

The current Mass also invites an exchange of peace with Offerte vōbīs pācem. The Agnus Dei, Īte, missa est, Deō grātiās, and the blessing Benedīcat vōs omnipotēns Deus keep the same Latin.

qs: The Mass is finished in heaven
